name: Lloyd Barenblatt
bio: Lloyd Barenblatt was a former Vassar College psychology instructor convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing, on First Amendment grounds, to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee's questions about alleged Communist associations. Sentenced to six months and a $250 fine, his case became the landmark Barenblatt v. United States (1959).
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Convicted; conviction upheld on appeal (1957); on appeal to the Supreme Court

name: Arthur McPhaul
bio: Arthur McPhaul was a Black Detroit labor and civil-rights figure, a former official of the Michigan Civil Rights Congress, convicted of contempt of Congress in December 1956 for refusing in 1952 to surrender the organization's books and records to the House Un-American Activities Committee. His case became McPhaul v. United States.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to surrender Civil Rights Congress records to HUAC

name: Hugo DeGregory
bio: Hugo DeGregory was a one-time Communist candidate for lieutenant-governor of Massachusetts, jailed for civil contempt in New Hampshire for refusing — even after a grant of immunity — to answer Attorney General Louis Wyman's questions about Communist associations. He challenged the state's immunity statute in the case that became DeGregory v. Attorney General of New Hampshire.
charges: Contempt — for refusing to answer a New Hampshire subversion probe
convicted: Ordered jailed until he answered; challenging the immunity law

name: Abraham Flaxer
bio: Abraham Flaxer was the president of the United Public Workers union, convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to give the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee the names of his union's roughly 30,000 members. His conviction was sent back for reconsideration after the 1957 Watkins decision (Flaxer v. United States).
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to surrender union membership lists
convicted: Convicted; remanded for reconsideration after Watkins (1957)

name: Marcus Singer
bio: Marcus Singer was a Cornell University zoologist indicted for contempt of Congress — at the same time as John Watkins in 1954 — for refusing to name past associates before the House Un-American Activities Committee. His conviction was reversed in July 1957 in the wake of the Supreme Court's Watkins ruling, and he was reinstated to the Cornell faculty.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to name associates before HUAC
